The runner returns the number of failures, errors and unexpected successes the result recorded, and the command ends the process with status 1 if there are any ([The runner: the test command and `DiscoverRunner`](testing/runner.md); `django/core/management/commands/test.py:Command.handle`).
`DiscoverRunner.run_tests` calls the runner's own methods in a fixed order, each of which a subclass may replace (`django/test/runner.py:DiscoverRunner.run_tests`):

`setup_test_environment` adds `"testserver"`, the host the test client's requests name, to `ALLOWED_HOSTS`; sets `settings.DEBUG` to what the runner passes, false unless the run was asked for `--debug-mode`; points the mailers (every alias of `MAILERS`, or `EMAIL_BACKEND` where a project has none) at the backend that keeps messages in a list in memory, the outbox; and replaces the method that renders a template of Django's own language, `_render`, on both the template's class and the partial's, with one that first sends the signal `template_rendered`, which the client listens to, and `assertTemplateUsed` as a context manager ([The test environment: `setup_test_environment`](testing/environment.md); `django/test/utils.py:setup_test_environment`).

The runner then reorders what it found, by default: any module or name that failed to load first, then the `TestCase` classes, then the other classes built on `SimpleTestCase`, then plain `unittest` tests; Django's documentation gives the reason as guaranteeing that every `TestCase` starts with a clean database (`docs/topics/testing/overview.txt`).
The tests of one class are kept together ([Finding and ordering the tests: `DiscoverRunner.build_suite`](testing/discovery.md); `django/test/runner.py:reorder_tests`).

Each test class names them in its `databases` attribute, empty on `SimpleTestCase` and `"default"` alone on `TransactionTestCase` and so on `TestCase`, and the runner collects them from every test of the suite ([Which databases a test uses: `databases`](testing/test-databases.md); `django/test/runner.py:DiscoverRunner._get_databases`, `django/test/utils.py:get_unique_databases_and_mirrors`).

Each test class names them in its `databases` attribute, empty on `SimpleTestCase` and `"default"` alone on `TransactionTestCase` and so on `TestCase`, and the runner collects them from every test of the suite ([Which databases a test uses: `databases`](testing/test-databases.md); `django/test/runner.py:DiscoverRunner._get_databases`, `django/test/utils.py:get_unique_databases_and_mirrors`).
The system checks run after this, a comment in the runner saying that some of them need the database (`django/test/runner.py:DiscoverRunner.run_checks`).

The hooks are Django's rather than the project's, so a test class that overrides `setUp` without calling the parent's loses none of them (`django/test/testcases.py:SimpleTestCase._setup_and_call`; [One test, in order: `SimpleTestCase`](testing/simple-test-case.md), which has the exceptions: a test marked skipped gets neither hook, one whose `_pre_setup` raises gets nothing more, and a `TransactionTestCase` that is not a `TestCase` runs its first test's `_pre_setup` in `setUpClass`).

Its `databases` is empty by default, and as each class is set up, every connection of the setting-up thread whose alias it does not name has its methods that connect or open a cursor replaced with ones that raise `DatabaseOperationForbidden`, an `AssertionError` whose message says to subclass `TestCase` or `TransactionTestCase`, or to add the alias to `databases`; for the length of the class, opening a connection to such an alias in another thread is refused too (`django/test/testcases.py:SimpleTestCase._add_databases_failures`).

After each test it runs the flush command on each of its databases that is not a mirror, which empties the models' tables (under `available_apps`, those applications'), and before each test it loads the class's fixtures again ([Emptying the tables after each test: `TransactionTestCase`](testing/transaction-test-case.md); `django/test/testcases.py:TransactionTestCase._fixture_teardown`).

Where its databases have transactions and savepoints, as the class is set up it opens an atomic block on each of them, loads the class's fixtures and calls `TestCase.setUpTestData`, all inside it; before each test it opens another atomic block inside the first, which is a savepoint; and after each test it rolls that back, and after the last the outer block too (`django/test/testcases.py:TestCase.setUpClass`, `django/test/testcases.py:TestCase._fixture_setup`).

Where its databases have transactions and savepoints, as the class is set up it opens an atomic block on each of them, loads the class's fixtures and calls `TestCase.setUpTestData`, all inside it; before each test it opens another atomic block inside the first, which is a savepoint; and after each test it rolls that back, and after the last the outer block too (`django/test/testcases.py:TestCase.setUpClass`, `django/test/testcases.py:TestCase._fixture_setup`).

The docstring of `LiveServerTestCase`, whose server answers in another thread, gives that as the reason it is a `TransactionTestCase`: threads do not share transactions, so each must commit for the other to see its rows; with SQLite's database in memory the test hands the server's thread its own connection, and the two share one ([A server in a thread: `LiveServerTestCase`](testing/live-server.md); `django/test/testcases.py:LiveServerTestCase`).

The handler builds its middleware chain at the client's first request, from the settings as they are then, and keeps it for the client's life; it sends each request through the chain to the view much as a server's handler would, though not quite: it sets no script prefix, leaves the test's database connections open, and returns the response object itself, its body emptied where a server would send none (`django/test/client.py:ClientHandler.__call__`).

It raises that exception again in the test, unless the client was made with `raise_request_exception=False`; otherwise it gives the response the templates and the contexts, the arguments the request was built from, a `json` function and a `resolver_match` worked out from the path when first read, and keeps the cookies the response set, so that the next request sends them, a session's among them, unless it gives a `"Cookie"` header of its own (`django/test/client.py:Client.request`).

The override stacks a holder of the new values on top of the settings and sends `setting_changed` for each name, and receivers, most of them in `django/test/signals.py`, repair what Django built from the old value, most by throwing it away: the URL resolvers' caches for `ROOT_URLCONF`, the template engines for `TEMPLATES`, the translations for `LANGUAGES` ([Overriding settings](startup/overrides.md)).

`teardown_test_environment` restores `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `settings.DEBUG`, the mail setting it replaced and the template renderer, and deletes the outbox (`django/test/utils.py:teardown_test_environment`).
